questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $k{x}^{2}(x-5)\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $k$ is a positive constant. If $P$ has velocity $v=2\sqrt{3}\,m/s$ at the origin and the particle is at rest when its displacement is $6\,m,$ find the value of $k.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14251337/assets/9ac139d8823f326f32869f308cb2d04cdc9e0d86dba7d4a11b66955afd665da3.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $k{x}^{2}(x-5)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=k{x}^{2}(x-5).
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=k{x}^{2}(x-5).
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int k({x}^{3}-5{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=k(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}-\frac{5{x}^{3}}{3})+C.
$$

Now, since $v=2\sqrt{3}\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}-\frac{5{x}^{3}}{3})+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2\sqrt{3})^{2} & =k(\frac{(0)^{4}}{4}-\frac{5(0)^{3}}{3})+C \\ C & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=k(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}-\frac{5{x}^{3}}{3})+6.
$$

Finally, since $v=0\,m/s$ when $x=6\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}-\frac{5{x}^{3}}{3})+6 \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & =k(\frac{(6)^{4}}{4}-\frac{5(6)^{3}}{3})+6 \\ 0 & =k(324-360)+6 \\ 0 & =-36k+6 \\ 36k & =6 \\ k & =\frac{1}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the positive $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ the magnitude of the acceleration is $\frac{k}{x+1}\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $k$ is a positive constant, and the acceleration is directed toward $O.$ If $P$ has velocity $v=4\,m/s$ at the origin and the particle is at rest when its displacement is $({e}^{4}-1)\,m,$ find the value of $k.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14251337/assets/e938c4ba0e20c0714d1cd0ef62fb6596b37341b06d29de4e675981007610e12a.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $\frac{k}{x+1}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{k}{x+1}.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-\frac{k}{x+1}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (-\frac{k}{x+1})\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-k\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+C.
$$

Now, since $v=4\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-k\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =-k\operatorname{ln}⁡(0+1)+C \\ C & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=8-k\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1).
$$

Finally, since $v=0\,m/s$ when $x=({e}^{4}-1)\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8-k\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1) \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & =8-k\operatorname{ln}⁡(({e}^{4}-1)+1) \\ k\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{4}) & =8 \\ 4k & =8 \\ k & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x\ge 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $(6-6x)\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has velocity $v=2\sqrt{2}\,m/s$ at the origin, find the maximum velocity of the particle.
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14251337/assets/61388466bb2d97b5080707e769ae862e633bfb0fe1d2b5f16c75daa14da76e53.png)

The extrema of the velocity occur at the critical points of $v.$ Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(6-6x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=6-6x.
$$

To find the moments where $v$ is a maximum, we need to solve $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}6-6x & =0 \\ x & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $x=1\,m.$

We now test the extreme value using the first derivative test. We summarize the necessary information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $(0,1)$ | $1$ | $(1,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $\frac{1}{2}$ |  | $2$ |
| $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ | $3>0$ | $0$ | $-6<0$ |
| $v$ | $↗$ | max | $↘$ |

We conclude that the velocity is maximized when $x=1\,m.$

Next, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our initial equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=6-6x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (6-6x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=6x-3{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=2\sqrt{2}\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =6x-3{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2\sqrt{2})^{2} & =6(0)-3(0)^{2}+C \\ C & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =6x-3{x}^{2}+4 \\ {v}^{2} & =12x-6{x}^{2}+8 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{-6{x}^{2}+12x+8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can disregard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=\sqrt{-6{x}^{2}+12x+8}.
$$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{max}=v(1)=\sqrt{-6(1)^{2}+12(1)+8}=\sqrt{14}\,m/s
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x\ge 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $k(4-2x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $k$ is a positive constant. If $P$ has velocity $v=4\,m/s$ at the origin and has velocity $v=8\,m/s$ when its displacement is $1\,m,$ find the maximum velocity of the particle.
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14251337/assets/73da2be2514373e6d0b1052f0eca21c339b4d826d38621faf72b3e251d7d8a95.png)

The extrema of the velocity occur at the critical points of $v.$ Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $k(4-2x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=k(4-2x).
$$

To find the moments where $v$ is a maximum, we need to solve $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ and test each solution using the first derivative test.

Solving $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}k(4-2x) & =0 \\ 4-2x & =0 \\ x & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $x=2\,m.$

We now test the extreme value using the first derivative test. We summarize the necessary information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $(0,2)$ | $2$ | $(2,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $1$ |  | $3$ |
| $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ | $2k>0$ | $0$ | $-2k<0$ |
| $v$ | $↗$ | max | $↘$ |

We conclude that the velocity is maximized when $x=2\,m.$

Next, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our initial equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=k(4-2x).
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int k(4-2x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=k(4x-{x}^{2})+C.
$$

Now, since $v=4\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k(4x-{x}^{2})+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =k(4(0)-(0)^{2})+C \\ C & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=k(4x-{x}^{2})+8.
$$

Also, since $v=8\,m/s$ when $x=1\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k(4x-{x}^{2})+8 \\ \frac{1}{2}(8)^{2} & =k(4(1)-{(1)}^{2})+8 \\ 32 & =3k+8 \\ 3k & =24 \\ k & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8(4x-{x}^{2})+8 \\ \frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =32x-8{x}^{2}+8 \\ {v}^{2} & =-16{x}^{2}+64x+16 \\ v & =\pm 4\sqrt{-{x}^{2}+4x+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can disregard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=4\sqrt{-{x}^{2}+4x+1}.
$$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{max}=v(2)=4\sqrt{-(2)^{2}+4(2)+1}=4\sqrt{5}\,m/s
$$

questions.problem:
A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\,m/s,$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $6x\,{m/s}^{2},$ and the acceleration is directed toward $O.$
If $P$ has velocity $4\,m/s$ when its displacement is $2\,m,$ find the values of $x$ for which $P$ is instantaneously at rest.
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14251337/assets/fa329a81ac533c3ab4bfd9ca6fb5b2ef81ff4e29fb8ff7f030c5e04952d9448d.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $6x\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-6x.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-6x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (-6x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-3{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=4\,m/s$ when $x=2\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-3{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =-3(2)^{2}+C \\ C & =8+12 \\ C & =20\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=20-3{x}^{2}.
$$

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when $v(x)=0\,m/s.$ We find the displacement of the particle when instantaneously at rest by substituting $v=0$ in the equation above and solving for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =20-3{x}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & =20-3{x}^{2} \\ {x}^{2} & =\frac{20}{3} \\ x & =\pm \frac{2}{3}\sqrt{15}\,m.\end{aligned}
$$
